en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Food, 32.
The Training Rule on Eating in a Group.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, Devadatta, having lost his gains and honor, ate by repeatedly making requests from families along with his retinue.
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about:
"How can these ascetics, sons of the Sakyans, eat by repeatedly making requests from families?"
"To whom is what is well-prepared not pleasing? To whom does what is delicious not appeal?
The monks heard those people complaining, grumbling, and resenting this.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... they complained, grumbled, and resented it.
“How indeed can Devadatta, together with his retinue, eat by repeatedly making requests at families?
… [and so on] … “Is it true, Devadatta, that you, together with your retinue, eat by repeatedly making requests at families?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, together with your retinue, eat after having repeatedly requested food from families?
This, foolish man, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And so, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“In eating in a group, there is an offense of expiation.
In this way, this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, people invited sick monks for a meal.
Being afraid of wrongdoing, the monks did not accept, thinking, “The Blessed One has prohibited eating in a group.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma on this occasion and in this context, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu who is ill, to eat a meal in a group.
And furthermore, bhikkhus, you should recite this training rule thus:”
“Eating in a group, except on the proper occasion, is an offense entailing expiation.
Herein, this is the proper occasion: the occasion of illness—this is the proper occasion therein.
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, when it was the season for giving robes, people prepared meals together with robes and invited the monks,
saying, "Having fed you, we shall clothe you with robes.
The monks, being afraid of wrongdoing, did not accept, thinking, "Eating in a group has been prohibited by the Blessed One."
A small robe was obtained.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One...
[as before] ... "I allow you, monks, to eat a meal in a group at the time of giving robes."
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:
“Eating in a group, except on an appropriate occasion, is an offense entailing confession.
Herein, this is the appropriate occasion: the occasion of illness, the occasion of the distribution of robes—this is the appropriate occasion therein.”
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, people invited bhikkhus who were making robes to a meal.
The bhikkhus, being afraid of wrongdoing, did not accept, thinking, “Eating in a group has been forbidden by the Blessed One.”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One...
[as before] ... "I allow you, monks, to eat a meal in a group at the time of making robes.
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:"
“Eating in a group, except on the proper occasions, is an offense entailing expiation.
Herein, these are the proper occasions: the occasion of illness, the occasion of the distribution of robes, and the occasion of making robes—this is the proper occasion there.
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, monks were traveling along a road together with people.
Then those monks said this to those people:
"Wait a moment, friends; we shall go for alms."
They said to him, “Venerable sir, please eat right here.
But the bhikkhus, being afraid of wrongdoing, did not accept, thinking, “The Blessed One has prohibited eating in a group.”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One...
[as before] ... "I allow you, monks, to eat a meal in a group when on a journey.
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:"
“Eating in a group, except on the proper occasions, is an offense entailing expiation.

Herein, these are the proper occasions: the occasion of illness, the occasion of the distribution of robes, the occasion of making robes, and the occasion of traveling on a journey—this is the proper occasion there.
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, monks were traveling by boat with people.
Then those monks said this to those people: “Friends, please bring us to the shore for a moment; we will go for alms.
They replied: “Venerable sirs, eat right here.”
The monks, being afraid of wrongdoing, did not accept [the food], thinking, “Group meals have been forbidden by the Blessed One.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One... [and the Blessed One said:
“I allow you, monks, to eat a group meal at the time of boarding a boat.”
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:
“Eating in a group, except on an appropriate occasion, is an offense entailing expiation.

Herein, this is the appropriate occasion: the occasion of illness, the occasion of the distribution of robes, the occasion of making robes, the occasion of traveling on a journey, the occasion of boarding a boat—this is the appropriate occasion therein.”
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, bhikkhus who had completed the rains retreat in various directions were coming to Rājagaha to see the Blessed One.
Seeing bhikkhus from various kingdoms, people invited them to a meal.
Being afraid of wrongdoing, the monks did not consent, saying, “Group meals have been forbidden by the Blessed One.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Blessed One said:
“I allow you, monks, to eat a group meal on a special occasion.”
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:
“In eating in a group, except on an appropriate occasion, there is an offense of expiation.

Herein, this is the appropriate occasion: the occasion of illness, the occasion of the distribution of robes, the occasion of making robes, the occasion of traveling on a journey, the occasion of boarding a boat, and the occasion of a great assembly—this is the appropriate occasion therein.”
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, a kinsman of King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha had gone forth among the Ājīvakas.
Then that Ājīvaka went to where King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha was.
Having approached King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, he said this to him: “Great King, I wish to provide food for all the various religious sects.
“Venerable sir, if you would first feed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with the Buddha at its head.”
“I shall do so. Then that Ājīvaka sent a messenger to the presence of the monks, saying: “May the monks accept my meal for tomorrow.
The monks, being apprehensive, did not accept it, thinking: “Group meals have been forbidden by the Blessed One.”
Then that Ājīvaka approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after exchanging polite and amiable words of greeting, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, that Ājīvaka said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama has gone forth, and I too have gone forth;
it is fitting for one who has gone forth to accept alms from another who has gone forth.
May Master Gotama, together with the community of monks, consent to accept a meal from me tomorrow.”
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then that Ājīvaka, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, departed.
Then, on this occasion and in this context, the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, monks, to eat a meal in a group at the time of a meal for ascetics.
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:
‘In eating in a group, except on an appropriate occasion, there is an offense of expiation.’”

"In this regard, these are the exceptions: the time of illness, the time of giving robes, the time of making robes, the time of traveling on a journey, the time of boarding a boat, the time of a great assembly, and the time of a meal for ascetics—these are the exceptions therein.
"A group meal" means:
where four bhikkhus, invited by someone with any one of the five kinds of cooked food, eat that food. This is what is called a "group meal."
"Except on an occasion" means excluding an occasion.
What is called "an occasion of illness"?
Even if one’s feet have cracked, one may eat [at that time], thinking, “It is the time of illness.
“The time for giving robes” means:

when the *kathina* has not been spread, it is the last month of the rainy season; when the *kathina* has been spread, it is the five months [following]. Thinking, “It is the time for giving robes,” one may eat.
The "robe-making season" refers to the time when a robe is being made. One may eat [at that time], thinking, "It is the robe-making season.
The "journeying season" refers to...
“One shall eat thinking: ‘I will go half a yojana’; one must eat while going; one must eat having gone.
The time for boarding a boat is: one shall eat thinking: ‘I will board a boat’; one must eat having boarded; one must eat having disembarked.”
“Great assembly” (mahāsamaya) means:
where two or three bhikkhus, having gone for alms, can sustain themselves, but when a fourth arrives, they cannot. “It is a great assembly”—one may eat there.
“The time of the alms-food of recluses” (samaṇabhattasamaya) means:
If anyone who has entered the state of a wandering ascetic prepares a meal, one may eat it thinking, "It is the time for the alms-food of the recluses.
If one accepts it with the intention, "I will eat it at another time," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one eats a group meal while perceiving it as a group meal, except on an appropriate occasion, one commits an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
If one eats a group meal while being doubtful about it, except on an appropriate occasion, one commits an offense entailing expiation.
If one eats a group meal while not perceiving it as a group meal, except on an appropriate occasion, one commits an offense entailing expiation.
If it is not a group meal, but one perceives it as a group meal, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is not a group meal, but one is doubtful about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not a group meal, and one perceives it as not a group meal, there is no offense.
There is no offense:
at the proper time,
or when two or three eat together.
Having wandered for alms, they gather together in one place and eat;
[this includes] regular meals and meals by ticket.
The fortnightly [meal],
the Uposatha [meal],
and the first-day-of-the-month [meal].
Except for the five kinds of food, there is no offense in all other cases;
nor is there an offense for one who is insane or for a first-time offender.
The training rule on eating in a group, the second, is concluded.
